newsitem.title: USA: Japan fundamentals justify yen level, IMF says.
newsitem.headline: Japan fundamentals justify yen level, IMF says.

text.p: The strong yen is justified by Japan's robust fundamentals and Tokyo should keep a lid on short-term interest rates to give its economic revival a chance, the International Monetary Fund said on Wednesday.
"Directors believed that the current level of the yen was broadly in line with fundamentals," the IMF's Executive Board said in its annual review of the Japanese economy.

"Directors believed that the current easy stance of monetary policy should be maintained for the time being, but that it would likely be desirable to begin tightening later in the year," the report added.

The IMF added it saw no reason yet to worry about Japan's current account surplus but warned of possible retaliation by Japan's trading partners should the surplus begin to rise in a sustained fashion.
U.S. officials have consistently urged Japan to ensure its recovery is led by domestic demand and not to let its current account surplus surge past 2.5 percent of gross domestic product.

A Japanese international finance official declined to comment on the yen's level or any of the IMF's specific recommendations, but told reporters in Washington he expected the nation's current account surplus to increase more slowly in the future than it had over the past few months.

"The current account has been rising in the past couple of months but we do not see any structural elements there, so we think the increase would slow down," the source, who asked not to be identified, told reporters.
The official spoke after an informal meeting between Japan's Vice Finance Minister for International Affairs Eisuke Sakakibara and U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers.
Both the Treasury and Sakakibara said in statements they had discussed a wide range of issues, including exchange rate policy, but declined to give any details.
A source close to the talks said she was unable to say whether the two had discussed specific dollar/yen levels.

Japanese short-term rates have been at historic lows for almost two years, helping the country to emerge from a spell of weak growth in 1995. GDP growth accelerated to 3.5 percent last year, one of highest rates in the industrial world, compared to just 1.5 percent in 1995.

The IMF said Japan's economic revival now appeared to be self-sustaining, but it urged the government to maintain its tight grip on spending and continue unwinding the fiscal stimulus package orginally aimed at aiding the recovery.
"The central challenge for policymakers (is) to return the fiscal balance to a more sustainable balance over the medium term," the report noted.
"Directors endorsed the fiscal correction measures enacted in the 1997 budget deficit as a step in the right direction."

The government earlier this year raised the consumption tax rate, withdrew a range of temporary tax cuts and pledged a range of spending cuts for the 1998 fiscal year in a bid to reduce its huge budget deficit.
Government reports say the Japanese economy is recovering gradually, even though the tax increases caused a temporary slowdown in April.

The fund urged Japan to keep up the pace of deregulation and structural reform to ensure robust growth in the long-term. It said one of the key issues for the government to address was the health of the country's banking sector.
"Directors welcomed the progress made over the past year in addressing financial sector problems, but noted that the strengthening of the banking system should remain a top priority," it said.
